intro.title: Start Here
intro.lede: A short orientation for teachers new to Wewoka High — what a walk-through looks for, what belongs on your board, how to unpack a standard, and how the curriculum and your resources relate. Watch each short video and skim the notes.

principalLookFors.description: A quick, honest picture of what walk-throughs are checking — bell-to-bell instruction, a posted objective, cognitive work by students, and feedback tied to a criterion.

curriculumVsResources.title: Curriculum vs. resources
curriculumVsResources.description: Your curriculum is the plan; your textbook and worksheets are tools. Don’t confuse the two — the standard drives the plan, and your resources serve the standard.

items.subject: Reading fluency
items.format: 15-minute session; 1:1 or small group
items.description: A structured fluency routine: adult models a passage, student does repeated readings, errors get phrase-drill correction, then a retell check and reward. Well-studied for struggling readers.

items.subject: Reading fluency
items.format: ~15 min; groups of up to 3; 2–3 times per week
items.description: A short, high-dosage fluency routine for a small group: passage preview, three repeated readings, phrase-drill error correction, and a contingent reward. Works when passages are at each student’s instructional level (~90% accuracy).

items.name: Reciprocal Teaching
items.subject: Reading comprehension
items.format: Small group; each student rotates through four roles
items.description: Students take turns leading a discussion using the four moves — predict, question, clarify, summarize — while working through a shared text. Builds active comprehension habits that transfer to independent reading.

items.subject: Reading comprehension
items.format: Small group or whole class; can be paired with any text
items.description: Teaches students to recognize four question types (Right There, Think & Search, Author & Me, On My Own) and where the answer lives. Immediately improves how students attack test questions and reading tasks.

items.subject: Math conceptual understanding
items.format: Small group or 1:1; multiple sessions per concept
items.description: Teach a new concept first with a physical object (concrete), then with a drawing or picture (representational), then with numbers and symbols (abstract). The bridge from physical to symbolic is where struggling learners break down — CRA rebuilds it.

items.format: Small group or 1:1; explicit modeling → guided → independent
items.description: Give students a named, step-by-step strategy for attacking word problems — teacher models it aloud (think-aloud), students practice with feedback, then release. WWC-reviewed.

items.subject: Math computation & problem solving

items.description: Structured peer tutoring. Students alternate the Coach and Player roles working through a set problem sequence. Everyone gets more practice repetitions than a teacher-led lesson can provide alone.

items.description: Direct, explicit practice of a small set of facts with 1-minute timings, immediate feedback, and a visible progress chart. Best used in short blocks alongside conceptual instruction, not as a substitute for it.

items.description: A structured approach that teaches students both a writing strategy (e.g., POW for planning; TREE for persuasive essays) and self-regulation habits (goal setting, self-monitoring). One of the most-studied writing interventions.

items.subject: Work completion, organization, engagement
items.format: Brief daily; mentor check-in AM + check-out PM; teacher point sheet
items.description: Student picks up a daily point sheet from a mentor before school. Teachers rate agreed-upon behaviors each period (in class, on task, work turned in). Student checks out at the end of the day. Fast to set up, high dosage, works well for the “on the bubble” students.

items.name: SIPPS — Systematic Instruction in Phonological Awareness, Phonics, and Sight Words
items.subject: Foundational decoding & phonics
items.format: 30 min, 4–5x/week, small group of 3–7 placed by a mastery test
items.description: A published, mastery-based decoding program with placement tests and short scripted routines: sound-by-sound blending, high-frequency word practice, spelling dictation, and a decodable text read. Move students on only after mastery, so a stuck reader repeats the routine (not the whole level) until it clicks. SIPPS Plus and Challenge Level use grade 4–12 texts so older students aren't reading kindergarten stories.

items.name: Wilson Reading System (WRS)
items.subject: Structured-literacy decoding & spelling for students with severe reading difficulty
items.format: 60–90 min, 4–5x/week, 1:1 or small group of 2–5; certified Wilson-trained teacher
items.description: An intensive Orton-Gillingham–based program built around a 10-part lesson: sound cards, word cards, sentence reading, controlled text, dictation, spelling. Every step is multisensory (tap the sounds, then blend). Best fit is the student who has already failed a lighter phonics intervention and needs the longer, more explicit sequence. WWC rates the evidence as mixed for adolescents — plan to progress-monitor decoding weekly and switch programs if you see no growth after ~30 sessions.

items.name: Robust Vocabulary Instruction (Text Talk / Bringing Words to Life)
items.subject: Academic (Tier 2) vocabulary
items.format: 10–15 min daily, small group or whole class; ~3 new words per read-aloud, revisited across the week
items.description: Pick 2–3 high-utility (Tier 2) words from an authentic text. After reading, contextualize the word in the story, give a kid-friendly definition, prompt students to use it in their own sentences, and revisit the word for 5–7 days in new contexts. When a student is stuck, add a quick example/non-example ("Is a puppy chasing its tail *frantic*? Is a cat napping *frantic*?") and a sentence frame to force use.

items.name: Heggerty Phonemic Awareness
items.subject: K–2 phonological & phonemic awareness
items.format: 10–12 min daily, whole class or small group of 4–6; scripted 35-week sequence
items.description: A fast, teacher-led oral warm-up moving through 8 phonemic-awareness skills each day — rhyming, onset-fluency, blending, isolating final sounds, segmenting, adding, deleting, substituting phonemes — all with hand motions and no worksheets. Runs before phonics as a listening bridge from sounds to letters. When a student can't hear the sounds, drop to two-phoneme words and increase modeling; when they can, extend into segmenting/manipulation with letter tiles.

items.name: REWARDS — Reading Excellence: Word Attack & Rate Development Strategies
items.subject: Multisyllabic decoding for grades 4–12
items.format: 20 lessons of ~50 min, 4–5x/week, small group of 3–8; short-term intervention (~5–6 weeks)
items.description: A short, scripted intervention that teaches older students a repeatable routine for attacking long words: find vowels, circle prefixes/suffixes, say the parts, say the whole word, check it makes sense. Designed by Anita Archer to plug a specific hole — students who can decode single-syllable words but stall on "transportation" or "unconstitutional." Pair the daily word-attack lesson with a passage read to build rate.

items.name: Number Talks (Small-Group Tier 2)
items.subject: Mental math & number sense
items.format: 10–15 min daily, small group of 4–6; one problem or string per day
items.description: Put one problem on the board (e.g., 48 + 25). Students solve mentally, put a thumb up when they have an answer, share strategies aloud while the teacher records each on the board. The goal is flexibility, not speed. In a Tier 2 group, keep the number range narrow (facts to 20 for early grades; fractions/percents strings for older) and make sure the student who never volunteers gets the first, easiest turn.

items.name: Cover-Copy-Compare (Math Fact Fluency)
items.subject: Math fact automaticity
items.format: 10 min, 4–5x/week, 1:1 or small group of 3–5; ~10 facts per session
items.description: Give the student a worksheet with 10 target facts + answers in the left column. Student studies one fact, covers it with an index card, writes it from memory in the right column, uncovers, checks. If correct, move on; if wrong, do the fact three more times before moving on. Fast, self-managed, brief timings — well studied for building automaticity without piling on stress.

items.name: Explicit Fraction Instruction (IES Fractions Guide)
items.subject: Conceptual fraction understanding, grades 3–8
items.format: 30–45 min, 3–4x/week, small group; number-line first, then operations
items.description: Teach fractions as numbers on a number line before teaching procedures. Sequence: build fractions with strips/tiles → place them on a number line → compare fractions with common numerator/denominator reasoning → then move to operations grounded in that meaning (not "keep-change-flip"). When a student is stuck on 3/4 + 1/2, back up to the number line and ask them to show each fraction with a strip before writing anything.

items.name: The Hochman Method — Sentence-Level Writing (The Writing Revolution)
items.subject: Sentence construction & academic writing
items.format: 10–20 min embedded daily across content classes; whole class or small group
items.description: A set of short, content-embedded sentence activities: sentence expansion using the who/what/when/where/why/how prompts, combining short sentences with because/but/so, appositives, and sentence types (statement, question, exclamation, command). The idea is to teach writing through sentences before paragraphs, using the material students are already learning in social studies or science — so writing practice doubles as content review.

items.name: POW + TREE (Elementary SRSD for Persuasive Writing)
items.subject: Persuasive writing, grades 2–5
items.format: 30–45 min, 3–4x/week, small group of 3–6; ~15–25 sessions across the SRSD six-stage cycle
items.description: The elementary version of SRSD: students learn POW (Pick an idea, Organize notes, Write and say more) as the general writing strategy, and TREE (Topic sentence, Reasons ≥3, Explain each, Ending) as the persuasive genre. Teacher models a full essay with a think-aloud, students memorize the mnemonics with games, then guided practice with self-talk cards, then independent writing with goal-setting. Distinct from secondary SRSD in the read-alouds, mnemonics practice, and heavy scaffolding of self-regulation.

items.name: Handwriting & Letter-Formation Intervention (e.g., Handwriting Without Tears)
items.subject: Letter formation, handwriting fluency (and downstream composition)
items.format: 10–15 min daily, whole class K–1 or small group / 1:1 for older struggling writers
items.description: Direct, brief practice of correct letter formation with a consistent verbal pathway ("big line down, little curve") and multi-sensory tools — wooden pieces, wet-dry-try slates, then paper. In older grades, target only the 6–8 letters a student reverses or forms inefficiently. The 2012 IES elementary writing guide flags handwriting fluency as a bottleneck for composition — automatic letter formation frees up working memory for what to say.

items.name: Check-In / Check-Out (CICO) — Behavior version
items.subject: On-task, respectful, following directions
items.format: Brief AM check-in (2–5 min) + teacher rating each period + PM check-out (5 min); daily
items.description: The behavior-focused version of CICO: student meets a mentor before school, picks up a Daily Progress Report with 3 school-wide expectations (e.g., Be Safe / Be Respectful / Be Responsible). Each period, the teacher rates 0/1/2 with a one-sentence comment. Student checks out at the end of the day, graphs the % of points earned, and takes the sheet home for a parent signature. Distinct from the academic CICO (work-completion focus) — the point sheet here targets behavior, and consequences for meeting the daily goal are social/tangible (praise, small privileges), not grades.

video.title: PBIS - Check-In/Check-Out, CICO, Tier 2

items.name: Behavior Contract with Home-School Note
items.subject: Targeted rule-following, work completion
items.format: Written contract negotiated once (~30 min); daily home-school note; weekly review meeting
items.description: Sit down with the student (and, when possible, the family) and write a 1-page contract in plain language: two or three specific behaviors to increase, how they'll be measured each day, and what the student earns for meeting the goal (privileges, notes home, points toward a reward). Send the daily home-school note home every afternoon. Fade the note frequency to weekly once the student hits the goal 4 of 5 days for two weeks running. Works best when the student helps pick the reinforcers.

video.title: What is a Behavioral Contract? Behavior Contracts EXPLAINED

resources.title: Intervention Central — Behavior Contracts
PBIS World — Tier 2 Behavior Contract

items.citation: Council for Exceptional Children — HLP #7 (establish a consistent, organized, and respectful learning environment). WWC single-case design evidence for daily behavior report cards (Vannest et al., 2010).

items.name: Self-Monitoring with Count-and-Graph
items.subject: On-task behavior, self-regulation
items.format: 10–15 min setup + daily use in one target period (e.g., 30 min of independent work)
items.description: Teach the student to notice and record their own target behavior. Pick one specific behavior (e.g., "working on my assignment"), set an audible cue (a beep app or a timer every 3–5 minutes), and have the student mark yes/no on a small tally card at each cue. Student graphs the daily percent at the end of the period, compares against their goal line, and confers with the teacher weekly. When the numbers stall, drop the interval (more cues), then fade back up. Works because the recording itself is reactive — awareness alone moves the behavior.

items.name: Success Mentor / Personalized Attendance Check-In
items.subject: Chronic absenteeism
items.format: 5–10 min daily greeting + 15 min weekly 1:1; mentor is a caring adult in the building
items.description: A named adult in the building — teacher, counselor, coach — is assigned to 5–15 students flagged by attendance data. They greet the student every morning by name, notice absences the same day, call home, and do a short weekly conference to problem-solve barriers (transportation, sleep, bullying, work). Data comes from the Early Warning System (ADA below 90%, plus grades and behavior). The mentor doesn't fix everything — they close the awareness loop and get the student connected to the right support.

video.title: Success Mentors to Address Chronic Absenteeism: A Four-Step Approach

resources.title: Attendance Works — Tackling Chronic Absence Through Mentoring

items.citation: Balfanz, R., & Byrnes, V. (2013). Meeting the Challenge of Combating Chronic Absenteeism. Everyone Graduates Center, Johns Hopkins University.

items.name: Positive Attendance Parent Messaging (Postcards/Nudges)
items.subject: Chronic absenteeism at scale
items.format: 5 mailings across the school year; automated print-and-mail or district-generated postcards
items.description: Mail a short, personalized postcard to families roughly every 6–8 weeks. It shows the student's actual absence count, a comparison with a typical peer ("your child has missed 12 days — most students in the class have missed 4"), and one specific action step. The Rogers & Feller study across 10 districts found this design cut chronic absenteeism by ~10% at less than $7 per student. Works because most parents underestimate how many days their child has missed.

video.title: Reducing Chronic Absenteeism and Improving Continued Attendance at the Start of the Year

resources.title: MDRC — Can Informing Parents Help High School Students Show Up for School?
FutureEd — Nudging Students and Families to Better Attendance

items.citation: Rogers, T., & Feller, A. (2018). Reducing student absences at scale by targeting parents' misbeliefs. Nature Human Behaviour, 2, 335–342.

items.name: WOOP — Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan
items.subject: Goal-setting, follow-through
items.format: 15–20 min small-group lesson to introduce; 3–5 min daily/weekly WOOP entry after that
items.description: A short goal-setting routine: student writes their Wish (one concrete academic goal for the week), the best Outcome if they achieve it, the main internal Obstacle in their way, and an if-then Plan ("If I feel like scrolling my phone after school, then I will put it in my backpack and open my math notebook"). Uses mental contrasting — you have to name the obstacle, not just visualize success. Works well as a Monday small-group routine paired with a Friday check-in.

video.title: WOOP Method

resources.title: Character Lab — WOOP for Classrooms
WOOP My Life (Oettingen)

items.name: Organized-Materials / Binder Check with Fading Support
items.subject: Organization of materials, homework completion
items.format: 5 min daily binder check; 10 min weekly full cleanout; fade to student-led over 6–8 weeks
items.description: Set up a single binder or folder system with named sections (Today, To-Turn-In, Graded/Keep, Reference). Every day, at the same time, a teacher or mentor spends 5 minutes checking the student's binder against the system. Weekly, the student cleans out — nothing loose, nothing crumpled, agenda updated. As accuracy climbs, move the check from daily to twice-weekly, then weekly, then student self-check with random spot-checks. The goal is not organization for its own sake — it's making the student's stuff findable so homework actually gets turned in.

items.name: Designated English Language Development (ELD) Block
items.subject: English language proficiency for MLs / newcomers
items.format: 30–45 min protected daily block, grouped by ELP level (e.g., WIDA 1–2, 3–4)
items.description: A protected daily block taught to a homogeneous group at the same English proficiency level. The block explicitly teaches language forms and functions — how to describe a process, ask a clarifying question, argue a claim — not just vocabulary. Lessons pair oral practice (structured discussion with a partner) with sentence frames and short writing. Distinct from Integrated ELD (which happens inside content classes); the designated block is where you go deep on the language itself.

items.name: Cognate Instruction Routine
items.subject: Vocabulary bridge from L1 (esp. Spanish) to English
items.format: 5–10 min daily bridge inside content lessons; small group or 1:1
items.description: Before reading a science or social studies passage, pre-teach 3–5 English words that share Latin/Greek roots with the student's home language (Spanish, Portuguese, French). Show the pair — *organización / organization*, *fotosíntesis / photosynthesis* — and ask the student to underline cognates as they read. Over time, students build a personal cognate chart and start noticing on their own. Especially high-leverage for Spanish-speaking MLs because 30–40% of academic English has a Spanish cognate.

items.citation: August, D., & Shanahan, T. (2006). Developing Literacy in Second-Language Learners: Report of the National Literacy Panel on Language-Minority Children and Youth. Lawrence Erlbaum.

items.name: Sentence-Frame Protocol for Academic Language
items.subject: Academic discussion & writing for MLs
items.format: Embedded in every content lesson; a small frame bank for the unit posted on the wall
items.description: Give students the language shell for the thinking you want. For a claim: "One reason ___ is ___." For agreeing/disagreeing: "I agree with ___ because ___," "I see it differently — ___." For comparing: "___ and ___ are alike because ___; they differ because ___." Model the frame, have partners rehearse it aloud, then hold students to using the frame in discussion and in writing. Fade the frames as students internalize the structure — but keep a bank posted for reference.

items.name: Good Behavior Game (GBG)
items.subject: Disruptive behavior, on-task classroom behavior
items.format: 10–20 min per round, 3–5x/week, teams of 4–6 within one class period; grows over the year
items.description: Split the class into two or three balanced teams. Post the 3–4 rules (e.g., stay seated during work time, hand up before speaking). During the game window, every rule infraction earns the team a mark on the board. Teams under a preset threshold (e.g., 4 marks) win — all winning teams get the reward. Start with short windows during your hardest transition, then extend. One of the most-replicated behavior interventions ever, with follow-up studies showing long-term reductions in aggression and later substance use.

items.name: Total Physical Response (TPR) for Newcomers
items.subject: Beginning English comprehension for newcomers (WIDA 1–2)
items.format: 10–15 min daily, whole newcomer class or small group of 4–8; comprehensible-input first, speech emerges later
items.description: Teacher gives short physical commands in English ("stand up," "pick up your book," "open to page 12") and models the action. Students listen and act — no speaking required. Once students can carry out commands reliably, vary the order, then chain commands ("stand up, walk to the window, point to the map"). Speech is not forced; students speak when they're ready. Especially valuable in the first weeks with a newcomer, before any productive language is realistic.

items.name: Cornell / Two-Column Note-Taking
items.subject: Note-taking, active study, comprehension of lectures & reading
items.format: 20–30 min explicit teaching + used across content classes; individual
items.description: A structured page: right column for notes taken live, narrow left column for cues/questions written afterward, bottom band for a 3–5-sentence summary. Teach in one sitting with a shared text or short lecture: model each column, do one together, release. Then require students to complete the left column and summary within 24 hours — that revisit is the actual learning move. Fold the notes on the vertical crease to self-quiz. Well-suited to Tier 2 study support in secondary classrooms.
